VIDEO.title: Matthew 13:1-23 – The SECRET Reason Jesus Told Parables!
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: He who has ears, let him hear.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 13:1-23, the start of Jesus' third discourse, the parables of the kingdom. Jesus tells the parable of the sower from a boat (13:3-9), explains why He speaks in parables (13:10-17), and explains the seed and the soils (13:18-23).

A parable is a story whose important characters illustrate a relevant lesson, felt through comparison. Jewish parables often opened with the formula 'To what may it be compared? It is like…', and Jesus does the same in 11:16. Quoting T. F. Torrance, the video says a parable throws the hearer into a 'crisis of decision,' yet its veiled form gives room and time to decide. We read the parable, and the parable reads us.

Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9-10. The crowds often understood the stories (Mark 12:12); they would not hear, and in Hebrew to hear is to obey. Four questions open any parable: What is the occasion? Who are the important characters? What do they say? What happens at the end?

The video adds four levels of Jewish interpretation, PaRDeS: peshat (the plain sense), remez (a hint back to the Old Testament), derash (a searched-out association, as Matthew 2:15 with Hosea 11:1), and sod (a secret only God reveals, as with Peter in 16:17).

Applied to the sower: the occasion is Jesus being challenged about His identity; the soils are the characters; the end is the good soil that hears, understands and bears fruit. So the question is not 'Am I the sower?' but 'Which soil am I?' The remez is 'understand with the heart': incline your heart to discernment (Proverbs 2:1-6; Psalm 119).
The lesson for the original audience: those who bear fruit for God's kingdom only do so as they continue to incline their heart to God's word.
QUOTES: The parable is also supposed to read us back.
To hear for a Hebrew meant to hear and to obey.
Those who bear fruit for God's kingdom only do so as they continue to incline their heart to God's word.
This exercise of the heart is a constant inclining.

PARABLES.title: The sower went out to sow

src.text: And He spoke many things to them in parables, saying, “Behold, the sower went out to sow; and as he sowed, some seeds fell beside the road, and the birds came and ate them up. And others fell on the rocky places, where they did not have much soil; and immediately they sprang up, because they had no depth of soil. But when the sun had risen, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away. And others fell among the thorns, and the thorns came up and choked them out. And others fell on the good soil and were yielding a crop, some a hundredfold, some sixty, and some thirty. He who has ears, let him hear.”

lines.text: Matthew 5-7 was the Sermon on the Mount; Matthew 10 the mission discourse. Chapter 13 is the parabolic discourse, teaching the disciples about the nature of the kingdom.
A parable is a story where the important characters illustrate a relevant lesson. Ancient Jewish parables often began, 'To what may it be compared? It is like…', as Jesus does in 11:16.

Quoting the Scottish theologian T. F. Torrance: the kingdom 'throws a man into the crisis of decision,' and yet by its veiled form the word 'holds a man at arms length away in order to give him room and time for personal decision.'
A parable invites you to step inside the story, find where you fit, and decide whether to adopt its lesson. We read the parable, and the parable reads us back.
Nathan's parable to David works the same way: 'You are the man!' (2 Samuel 12:7).

left.text: Render the hearts of this people insensitive, / Their ears dull, / And their eyes dim, / Lest they see with their eyes, / And hear with their ears, / And understand with their hearts, / And return and be healed.”

right.text: Therefore I speak to them in parables; because while seeing they do not see, and while hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand.

lines.text: Isaiah had just seen the Lord on His throne, and a seraph touched his lips to take away his guilt (Isaiah 6:1-7). Then God sent him to call out Israel's unwillingness to understand with the heart and turn.
The crowds often understood the stories. In Mark 12 the leaders 'understood that He spoke the parable against them' (Mark 12:12); they just would not hear. In Hebrew, to hear is to obey.
The Shema begins with this word: 'Hear, O Israel!' (Deuteronomy 6:4).
1. What is the occasion? Why is Jesus telling this story; what is He responding to?
2. Who are the important characters? Usually three, sometimes two, occasionally one. 3. What do they say out loud?
4. What happens at the end? Often an unexpected twist that grabs the listener so they understand and respond.

Peshat means simple: the surface meaning, the easiest to see. Western churches know it well, because pastors teach the plain sense of the passage every Sunday. It is fundamental, and the other levels never undermine it.
The video calls the four levels PaRDeS, an acronym (the captions hear 'partardes'): peshat, remez, derash, sod.

Remez means hint: a veiled allusion that sends you back to the Old Testament. Rabbis buried a remez like treasure, so students would go back and find the deeper framework. The journey was meant to take time.
In the sower, the remez is 'understand with the heart,' which runs through Proverbs 2 and Psalm 119.

left.text: When Israel was a youth I loved him, / And out of Egypt I called My son.

right.text: And he remained there until the death of Herod, in order that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet would be fulfilled, saying, “Out of Egypt I called My Son.”

lines.text: Derash means inquire or search: a meaningful association with an earlier passage, respecting the context of each, to draw out a lesson. Hosea 11:1 is about Israel, yet Matthew sees a real link between God's words and Joseph's actions.
Remez hints at treasure elsewhere; derash builds a lesson from it. Jesus does this throughout His parables.

src.text: And Jesus answered and said to him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but My Father who is in heaven.

lines.text: Sod means secret: understanding only God can give, which cannot be learned by rote. When Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, Jesus says the Father revealed it.
This is not about becoming Judaizers or chasing esoteric doctrines. It is about having ears to hear: respecting the Jewish way Jesus taught and His students learned.

Jesus had been challenged about His identity by John's disciples, the scribes and Pharisees, and others. He denounced the towns that rejected Him and corrected false expectations. 'On that day' (13:1) He began the parables, still in a corrective setting.

src.text: When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is the one on whom seed was sown beside the road. And the one on whom seed was sown on the rocky places, this is the man who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy; yet he has no root in himself, but is only temporary, and when affliction or persecution arises because of the word, immediately he falls away. And the one on whom seed was sown among the thorns, this is the one who hears the word, and the worry of the world and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.

lines.text: The sower is the setup, not the focus. 'The one on whom seed was sown… this is the one': the soils are the characters. They do not speak; they act out how seed does or does not produce grain.
So the parable is not mainly a call to see yourself as the sower spreading seed. The question is: which soil am I?

src.text: And the one on whom seed was sown on the good soil, this is the man who hears the word and understands it; who indeed bears fruit and brings forth, some a hundredfold, some sixty, and some thirty.”

lines.text: The end rests with the good soil, the one who hears and understands, and bears fruit. The unusual way Jesus counts the yield is, the video says, worth exploring on your own.
Isaac 'sowed in that land and reaped in the same year one hundredfold' (Genesis 26:12), a sign of God's blessing.

src.text: My son, if you will receive my words / And treasure my commandments within you, / To make your ear pay attention to wisdom, / Incline your heart to discernment; / For if you call out for understanding, / Give your voice for discernment; / If you seek her as silver / And search for her as for hidden treasures; / Then you will understand the fear of Yahweh / And find the knowledge of God. / For Yahweh gives wisdom; / From His mouth come knowledge and discernment.

right.text: Cause me to understand, that I may observe Your law / And keep it with all my heart.

lines.text: Following Reyburn and Fry, 'incline your heart' is a Hebrew idiom meaning commit yourself: work hard to understand. The heart is not the seat of emotions but of intellect and will, the center of the whole person.
Had the people committed themselves to understand, gone back to the word like the Bereans (Acts 17:11), they would have recognized their Messiah. There were no surprises in Jesus' teaching.

TERMS.def: A story whose important characters illustrate a relevant lesson, by comparison: 'It is like…'
Truths about God's kingdom once hidden and now revealed to disciples (13:11).
An acronym for four levels of Jewish interpretation: peshat, remez, derash, sod. The captions write 'partardes.'
The plain, surface meaning of a text.
A hint that sends the hearer back to an Old Testament passage. The captions write 'Rome.'
From 'to inquire, search': a lesson drawn from a meaningful link between passages. The captions write 'dash.'
A Hebrew idiom: commit yourself, work hard to understand (Proverbs 2:2).

WORDS.gloss: Parable, comparison, illustration. Look up: BDAG, παραβολή.
Rocky, with rock just below the soil.
To understand, put together. Look up: BDAG, συνίημι.
To make thick; of the heart, dull, insensitive.
To cause to stumble; passive, to fall away.
To stretch out, turn, incline. Look up: BDB or HALOT, נָטָה.
Heart: mind, will and inner self.

BACKGROUND.p: Farmers scattered seed by hand, often before plowing it in. Paths ran through fields, limestone lay close under thin soil in places, and thorn plants grew at the edges, so some seed was always lost.
Ancient yields were usually modest; a hundredfold was a mark of God's blessing, as for Isaac (Genesis 26:12). Jesus' numbers stress how abundant the good soil's fruit is.

Rabbinic literature contains many parables (meshalim), often introduced with 'To what may the matter be compared? To a king who…'. Most of the written examples are later than Jesus, but the form is old: compare Nathan's parable in 2 Samuel 12.

The four-level scheme and the acronym PaRDeS appear in medieval Jewish writings (13th century). The methods behind peshat and derash, and the use of allusion, are much older, and the video uses the four levels as a helpful lens.

WITNESSES.text: For by seed here He means His doctrine, and by land, the souls of men, and by the sower, Himself.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 44, on 13:3. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: Not through the sower, but through the ground that received it; that is, the soul that did not hearken.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 44, on 13:4-8. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: For if it had not been His will that they should hear and be saved, He ought to have been silent, not to have spoken in parables; but now by this very thing He stirs them up, even by speaking under a veil.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 45, on 13:13. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

DEBATES.p: Both, says 13:11-13: they reveal to those who want to hear and hide from those who refuse. Chrysostom: by 'speaking under a veil' Jesus stirs them up. Others stress God's judgment in the hiding, as in Isaiah 6.

The video: the soils are the focus, so ask 'Which soil am I?' Jesus' later explanation names the sower of good seed as the Son of Man (13:37), and many preachers also draw a lesson for those who share the word.
The acronym is medieval. Many scholars still find related moves in the New Testament: plain reading, allusion (remez), and searched-out application (derash, compare the Qumran pesharim).

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says the four levels were 'in the first century.' The acronym PaRDeS and the four-level scheme come from medieval Jewish writers (13th century); the underlying methods are older, so it is a helpful lens rather than a first-century system.

Matthew 13:14-15 follows the Greek Septuagint of Isaiah 6:9-10 ('the heart of this people has become dull'), while the Hebrew, as in the LSB, is a command: 'Render the hearts of this people insensitive.'
The quotations of T. F. Torrance and of Reyburn and Fry are given as the video reads them; we could not check them against the books.
The video reads Proverbs 2:2 as 'inclining your heart to understanding'; the LSB has 'Incline your heart to discernment.'
The captions write 'partardes' for PaRDeS, 'pashhat' for peshat, 'Rome' for remez, 'dash' for derash, 'Raburn' for Reyburn, and 'coin and Greek' for Koine Greek.

QUESTIONS: Which soil describes you right now: beside the road, rocky, thorny, or good? Why?
What 'worry of the world' is choking the word in your life this season?
How does 'to hear is to obey' change how you read 'He who has ears, let him hear'?
Pick a parable you know. Walk it through the four questions. What do you notice?
What would it look like to 'incline your heart' to God's word every day this week?
Where might your expectations of God be keeping you from hearing what He is actually saying?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: those who bear fruit for God's kingdom only do so as they continue to incline their heart to God's word. Jesus told this parable among people who refused to acknowledge His identity. They rejected Him because they would not let go of their expectations of what God and His Messiah would do; too proud to believe their reading of God's word was wrong, they would not go back to the Tanakh with an open mind. Had they committed themselves to understand, they would have seen that there were no surprises in Jesus' teaching: He came to fulfill what the Old Testament always taught. Inclining the heart leads a person through repentance and acceptance of the gospel, and further into obeying everything Jesus taught, the word of the kingdom, including the Sermon on the Mount and the Great Commission. It is a constant inclining, a daily discipline of returning to God's word with an open mind, ready for God to do things outside our expectations.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): this week, read Proverbs 2:1-6 each morning, then read one parable in Matthew 13 and walk it through the four questions. Write down one place where the parable 'read you back.'

## Four levels of interpretation
1. Peshat: The plain sense
   (video) Peshat means simple: the surface meaning, the easiest to see. Western churches know it well, because pastors teach the plain sense of the passage every Sunday. It is fundamental, and the other levels never undermine it.
   (video) The video calls the four levels PaRDeS, an acronym (the captions hear 'partardes'): peshat, remez, derash, sod.
2. Remez: A hint to the Tanakh
   (video) Remez means hint: a veiled allusion that sends you back to the Old Testament. Rabbis buried a remez like treasure, so students would go back and find the deeper framework. The journey was meant to take time.
   (video) In the sower, the remez is 'understand with the heart,' which runs through Proverbs 2 and Psalm 119.
3. Derash: Search out the connection
   Hosea (Hosea 11:1, LSB): "When Israel was a youth I loved him, / And out of Egypt I called My son."
   Matthew (Matthew 2:15, LSB): "And he remained there until the death of Herod, in order that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet would be fulfilled, saying, “Out of Egypt I called My Son.”"
   (video) Derash means inquire or search: a meaningful association with an earlier passage, respecting the context of each, to draw out a lesson. Hosea 11:1 is about Israel, yet Matthew sees a real link between God's words and Joseph's actions.
   (video) Remez hints at treasure elsewhere; derash builds a lesson from it. Jesus does this throughout His parables.
4. Sod: A secret God reveals
   Secret Matthew 16:17: "And Jesus answered and said to him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but My Father who is in heaven." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+16:17
   (video) Sod means secret: understanding only God can give, which cannot be learned by rote. When Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, Jesus says the Father revealed it.
   (video) This is not about becoming Judaizers or chasing esoteric doctrines. It is about having ears to hear: respecting the Jewish way Jesus taught and His students learned.

## Which soil am I?
1. Question 1: The occasion
   (video) Jesus had been challenged about His identity by John's disciples, the scribes and Pharisees, and others. He denounced the towns that rejected Him and corrected false expectations. 'On that day' (13:1) He began the parables, still in a corrective setting. (Matthew 11:2-6; Matthew 12:38)
2. Matthew 13:18-22: The soils are the characters
   Which soil? Matthew 13:19-22: "When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is the one on whom seed was sown beside the road. And the one on whom seed was sown on the rocky places, this is the man who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy; yet he has no root in himself, but is only temporary, and when affliction or persecution arises because of the word, immediately he falls away. And the one on whom seed was sown among the thorns, this is the one who hears the word, and the worry of the world and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+13:19-22
   (video) The sower is the setup, not the focus. 'The one on whom seed was sown… this is the one': the soils are the characters. They do not speak; they act out how seed does or does not produce grain.
   (video) So the parable is not mainly a call to see yourself as the sower spreading seed. The question is: which soil am I?
3. Matthew 13:23: The good soil
   Fruit Matthew 13:23: "And the one on whom seed was sown on the good soil, this is the man who hears the word and understands it; who indeed bears fruit and brings forth, some a hundredfold, some sixty, and some thirty.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+13:23
   (video) The end rests with the good soil, the one who hears and understands, and bears fruit. The unusual way Jesus counts the yield is, the video says, worth exploring on your own.
   [Background] Isaac 'sowed in that land and reaped in the same year one hundredfold' (Genesis 26:12), a sign of God's blessing. (Genesis 26:12)
4. Proverbs 2 and Psalm 119: Incline your heart
   Psalmist (Psalms 119:34, LSB): "Cause me to understand, that I may observe Your law / And keep it with all my heart."
   Remez Proverbs 2:1-6: "My son, if you will receive my words / And treasure my commandments within you, / To make your ear pay attention to wisdom, / Incline your heart to discernment; / For if you call out for understanding, / Give your voice for discernment; / If you seek her as silver / And search for her as for hidden treasures; / Then you will understand the fear of Yahweh / And find the knowledge of God. / For Yahweh gives wisdom; / From His mouth come knowledge and discernment." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Proverbs+2:1-6
   (video) Following Reyburn and Fry, 'incline your heart' is a Hebrew idiom meaning commit yourself: work hard to understand. The heart is not the seat of emotions but of intellect and will, the center of the whole person.
   (video) Had the people committed themselves to understand, gone back to the word like the Bereans (Acts 17:11), they would have recognized their Messiah. There were no surprises in Jesus' teaching. (Acts 17:11)

## Key people
- Jesus: Teaches from a boat in parables; the rabbi who sends His students back to the word. [Background] Matthew sees His parables as fulfilling Psalm 78:2: 'I will open My mouth in parables' (13:35).
- The crowds: Hear the stories; many understand them but will not hear and obey. [Background] They stood on the beach while He sat in the boat (13:2).
- The disciples: Ask why He speaks in parables; to them the mysteries are given. [Background] 'Blessed are your eyes, because they see' (13:16).
- The sower: The setup of the story, not its focus. [Background] Chrysostom reads the sower as Christ Himself, the seed as His teaching.
- The four soils: The real characters: beside the road, rocky places, thorns, and good soil. [Background] Jeremiah: 'Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns' (Jeremiah 4:3).
- Isaiah: Saw the Lord enthroned and was sent to a people who would not understand with the heart. [Background] John 12:39-41 and Acts 28:25-27 also quote Isaiah 6.

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: 'Jesus went out of the house and was sitting by the sea' (13:1); likely His house in Capernaum.
- Cove of the Parables: A natural inlet between Capernaum and Tabgha, traditionally linked with teaching from a boat (13:2); the site is tradition, not certain.
- Gennesaret: The fertile plain on the west shore: fields, paths, rocks and thorns like those in the parable.
- Magdala: A fishing town on the west shore.

## Key terms
- Parable: A story whose important characters illustrate a relevant lesson, by comparison: 'It is like…'
- Mysteries of the kingdom: Truths about God's kingdom once hidden and now revealed to disciples (13:11). [Background]
- PaRDeS: An acronym for four levels of Jewish interpretation: peshat, remez, derash, sod. The captions write 'partardes.'
- Peshat: The plain, surface meaning of a text.
- Remez: A hint that sends the hearer back to an Old Testament passage. The captions write 'Rome.'
- Derash: From 'to inquire, search': a lesson drawn from a meaningful link between passages. The captions write 'dash.'
- Sod: 'Secret': understanding only God can reveal (16:17).
- Incline the heart: A Hebrew idiom: commit yourself, work hard to understand (Proverbs 2:2).

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Sowing in Galilee: Farmers scattered seed by hand, often before plowing it in. Paths ran through fields, limestone lay close under thin soil in places, and thorn plants grew at the edges, so some seed was always lost.
- A good harvest: Ancient yields were usually modest; a hundredfold was a mark of God's blessing, as for Isaac (Genesis 26:12). Jesus' numbers stress how abundant the good soil's fruit is.
- Jewish parables: Rabbinic literature contains many parables (meshalim), often introduced with 'To what may the matter be compared? To a king who…'. Most of the written examples are later than Jesus, but the form is old: compare Nathan's parable in 2 Samuel 12.
- PaRDeS: The four-level scheme and the acronym PaRDeS appear in medieval Jewish writings (13th century). The methods behind peshat and derash, and the use of allusion, are much older, and the video uses the four levels as a helpful lens.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Do parables hide or reveal? Both, says 13:11-13: they reveal to those who want to hear and hide from those who refuse. Chrysostom: by 'speaking under a veil' Jesus stirs them up. Others stress God's judgment in the hiding, as in Isaiah 6.
- Is the sower us? The video: the soils are the focus, so ask 'Which soil am I?' Jesus' later explanation names the sower of good seed as the Son of Man (13:37), and many preachers also draw a lesson for those who share the word.
- Did first-century rabbis use PaRDeS? The acronym is medieval. Many scholars still find related moves in the New Testament: plain reading, allusion (remez), and searched-out application (derash, compare the Qumran pesharim).

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says the four levels were 'in the first century.' The acronym PaRDeS and the four-level scheme come from medieval Jewish writers (13th century); the underlying methods are older, so it is a helpful lens rather than a first-century system.
- Matthew 13:14-15 follows the Greek Septuagint of Isaiah 6:9-10 ('the heart of this people has become dull'), while the Hebrew, as in the LSB, is a command: 'Render the hearts of this people insensitive.'
- The quotations of T. F. Torrance and of Reyburn and Fry are given as the video reads them; we could not check them against the books.
- The video reads Proverbs 2:2 as 'inclining your heart to understanding'; the LSB has 'Incline your heart to discernment.'
- The captions write 'partardes' for PaRDeS, 'pashhat' for peshat, 'Rome' for remez, 'dash' for derash, 'Raburn' for Reyburn, and 'coin and Greek' for Koine Greek.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Which soil describes you right now: beside the road, rocky, thorny, or good? Why?
2. What 'worry of the world' is choking the word in your life this season?
3. How does 'to hear is to obey' change how you read 'He who has ears, let him hear'?
4. Pick a parable you know. Walk it through the four questions. What do you notice?
5. What would it look like to 'incline your heart' to God's word every day this week?
6. Where might your expectations of God be keeping you from hearing what He is actually saying?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: those who bear fruit for God's kingdom only do so as they continue to incline their heart to God's word. Jesus told this parable among people who refused to acknowledge His identity. They rejected Him because they would not let go of their expectations of what God and His Messiah would do; too proud to believe their reading of God's word was wrong, they would not go back to the Tanakh with an open mind. Had they committed themselves to understand, they would have seen that there were no surprises in Jesus' teaching: He came to fulfill what the Old Testament always taught. Inclining the heart leads a person through repentance and acceptance of the gospel, and further into obeying everything Jesus taught, the word of the kingdom, including the Sermon on the Mount and the Great Commission. It is a constant inclining, a daily discipline of returning to God's word with an open mind, ready for God to do things outside our expectations.
- Study note (added): this week, read Proverbs 2:1-6 each morning, then read one parable in Matthew 13 and walk it through the four questions. Write down one place where the parable 'read you back.'
